docs.title: PM-KISAN income support
docs.text: PM-KISAN gives every landholding farmer family Rs 6,000 per year in three equal instalments of Rs 2,000, paid directly to the bank account via DBT. Register at the nearest Common Service Centre or on the PM-KISAN portal with land records (RTC/Pahani), Aadhaar and a bank passbook. Instalments stop if the Aadhaar-bank link or e-KYC is not completed, so farmers should check their status every season.

docs.title: PMFBY crop insurance
docs.text: Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana (PMFBY) insures notified crops against drought, flood, pest attack and post-harvest loss. The farmer's premium is capped at 2% of sum insured for kharif crops, 1.5% for rabi, and 5% for commercial/horticulture crops; the rest is subsidised by the government. Enrol through your bank, CSC or insurance company before the cut-off date for that crop and season, and report crop loss within 72 hours through the app, helpline or insurance company for the claim to be valid.

docs.title: Kisan Credit Card (KCC)
docs.text: The Kisan Credit Card gives farmers short-term credit for crop production, post-harvest expenses and farm maintenance at a subsidised interest rate, effectively 4% per year if repaid on time (interest subvention scheme). It can be obtained from any nationalised bank or cooperative bank with land records and identity proof, and doubles as the account used for many DBT scheme payments.

docs.title: Soil Health Card scheme
docs.text: The Soil Health Card scheme tests a farmer's soil every 2 years for nutrients (N, P, K), pH, organic carbon and micronutrients, and gives crop-wise fertiliser recommendations. Samples can be submitted at the local Krishi Vigyan Kendra or agriculture department office; using the card's recommendations instead of guessing fertiliser doses typically cuts input cost while improving yield.

docs.title: e-NAM electronic mandi trading
docs.text: e-NAM (National Agriculture Market) links APMC mandis electronically so a farmer's lot can be bid on by traders beyond the local market, improving price discovery. Produce is graded on arrival, and payment is intended to reach the farmer's account within 24 hours of the deal. It works alongside, not instead of, physical mandi delivery.

docs.title: Minimum Support Price (MSP)
docs.text: MSP is the floor price the government guarantees for notified crops, announced before each sowing season for kharif and rabi separately. If the mandi price falls below MSP, farmers can sell to government procurement centres (FCI, NAFED or state agencies) instead of private traders, but this usually requires prior registration and a quality check against the notified grade.

docs.title: How APMC mandi selling works
docs.text: At an APMC mandi, produce is weighed and graded on arrival, then sold through open auction to licensed traders. The mandi charges a commission (usually 1-2%, varies by state and commodity) plus market fee, deducted before the farmer is paid. Always ask for the weighing slip and the trader's licence number, and check the day's modal price on the notice board before agreeing to a bid, since prices can swing 10-15% within the same day between arrival slots.

docs.title: Reducing middleman commission loss
docs.text: Selling directly to a verified buyer or bulk purchaser, or pooling produce through an FPO, removes one or more layers of commission compared to selling through multiple local traders. Farmers lose the most value when they sell in small, ungraded lots to the first buyer who visits the farm gate; grading produce (by size, moisture, damage) before sale typically raises the offered price.

docs.title: FPO pooling for small farmers
docs.text: A Farmer Producer Organisation (FPO) pools small quantities from many farmers into one large, uniformly graded lot, which attracts better per-quintal offers than each farmer selling alone, and can also negotiate shared transport to a farther but higher-paying market. Pooling works best when farmers agree on the same grade standard and delivery date; an under-graded lot from one member can lower the price for the whole pool.

docs.title: Protected/escrow payments in produce sale
docs.text: In an escrow-protected sale, the buyer's payment is held by a neutral third party until the farmer confirms the produce was received and accepted at the agreed grade and weight, then it is released. This protects the farmer from a buyer who takes delivery and delays or refuses payment, and protects the buyer from paying before verifying quality. Any weight or quality dispute should be raised immediately, with photos if possible, before the escrow is released.

docs.title: Onion storage and rot prevention
docs.text: Onion rot in storage is usually caused by harvesting before the neck has dried, high moisture at curing, or piling bulbs too deep without ventilation. Cure onions in a shaded, ventilated area for 10-15 days after harvest until the neck is fully dry, store in single layers or mesh bags rather than sacks, and remove any bulb showing soft rot or black mould immediately since it spreads to neighbouring bulbs.

docs.title: Onion pest and disease: thrips and purple blotch
docs.text: Thrips appear as silvery streaks on onion leaves and cause the tips to dry and curl; spraying with a systemic insecticide or neem-based product at the first sign, repeated after 10 days, controls most infestations. Purple blotch shows as purple-brown concentric spots on leaves during humid weather; a copper oxychloride or mancozeb-based fungicide spray, along with proper field drainage, reduces spread.

docs.title: Tur (arhar/pigeon pea) wilt and pod borer
docs.text: Fusarium wilt in tur shows as sudden yellowing and wilting of the whole plant, usually worse in fields cropped with tur repeatedly; using a wilt-resistant variety and a 3-year rotation with a non-legume crop is the main control since there is no cure once a plant is infected. Pod borer (Helicoverpa) damage appears as holes in pods with larvae inside; monitor with pheromone traps and spray only when larvae counts cross the threshold, to avoid killing natural predators unnecessarily.

docs.title: Cotton bollworm and whitefly management
docs.text: Pink and American bollworm attack cotton bolls from inside, so pheromone traps for early warning and timely spraying before boll formation are more effective than spraying after damage is visible. Whitefly buildup, especially in hot dry spells, also transmits cotton leaf curl virus; yellow sticky traps and neem-based sprays help, and spraying should be avoided during the hottest part of the day to protect natural predator insects.

docs.title: Kharif and rabi sowing windows
docs.text: Kharif crops (paddy, cotton, tur, groundnut, soybean) are sown with the onset of the south-west monsoon, roughly June to July in most of Karnataka, and need 600-1200mm of rain over the season. Rabi crops (wheat, jowar, gram, sunflower) are sown after the monsoon withdraws, roughly October to November, relying more on residual soil moisture and irrigation, and generally need less total rainfall (300-500mm).

docs.title: Managing red laterite soil
docs.text: Red laterite soils, common across much of Karnataka's plateau, are low in organic matter, nitrogen and phosphorus, and drain quickly, so they dry out fast between rains. Adding farmyard manure or compost improves water retention and nutrient content; DAP or single super phosphate at sowing corrects the typical phosphorus deficiency, and mulching between rows reduces moisture loss in the dry spells common on this soil type.

docs.title: Managing black cotton soil
docs.text: Black soil (regur) holds moisture and nutrients well and suits cotton, jowar and tur, but it cracks deeply when dry and becomes waterlogged and sticky when wet, so field drainage and correctly timed sowing (not right after heavy rain, not in a dry crust) matter more than fertiliser choice. Deep ploughing once every 2-3 years after harvest helps break up the compaction this soil type tends to form.

docs.title: What to do about a weighing or payment dispute
docs.text: If a buyer's recorded weight is lower than expected, ask to re-weigh in front of a witness on a certified scale before the produce leaves the yard; once it leaves, disputing the weight becomes much harder. For a payment that is late or short, keep the weighing slip, any photos, and the buyer's contact details, and raise a complaint through the mandi committee, FPO, or the marketplace platform's dispute process rather than accepting a lower amount under pressure.

docs.title: Why grading produce before sale matters
docs.text: Sorting produce by size, moisture content and visible damage before taking it to market, or before a buyer inspects it, usually raises the average price obtained, because ungraded lots are priced as if the whole lot were the worst quality present. Even simple grading into two tiers (good vs damaged/small) at the farm before transport can meaningfully change what a trader is willing to offer.

docs.title: Weather timing for spraying pesticide or fertiliser
docs.text: Avoid spraying pesticide or foliar fertiliser just before expected rain, since it washes off before absorption; the ideal window is early morning or late afternoon in calm, dry weather. Spraying during strong wind causes drift onto neighbouring plots, and spraying in the hottest part of a hot day can scorch leaves and reduce effectiveness of the chemical.
